summary: Defines the Simple Public-Key Mechanism, a way for programs using the Generic Security Service API to authenticate each other and protect messages using public-key cryptography.

plainLanguage.summary: SPKM is one way to fill in the security functions an application calls when it needs to authenticate a partner and protect a message. It uses certificates and public-key cryptography instead of a shared password, and it comes in two versions: one that needs a trusted clock and one that does not.

how does spkm authenticate with public keys
what is quality of protection in gss-api
subtitle: Lets a program use public-key certificates for authentication and message protection through the GSS-API.

tldr.problem: Kerberos works well where a shared secret can be installed on both sides, but some applications need a mechanism built on public keys instead, so that no shared secret has to be pre-arranged.
tldr.mechanism: SPKM is a GSS-API mechanism: the applications keep calling the same GSS-API functions, and the mechanism underneath uses X.509 certificates, RSA, and negotiated algorithm identifiers to authenticate the peers and to protect each message. It comes in two forms, SPKM-1 and SPKM-2, differing in whether secure timestamps are required.
tldr.outcome: SPKM-1 works without a trusted clock, and both forms offer true digital signatures, so a message can carry proof of who sent it. The formats and procedures are kept close to those of Kerberos, and the key management is meant to fit X.509 and PEM.

today: RFC 2025 is a Proposed Standard published in October 1996. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What SPKM Is For
sections.content:
The goal of the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface is to provide security services to callers in a generic fashion, supportable with a range of underlying mechanisms, so that applications are portable between environments. SPKM is a GSS-API Mechanism: a document that defines the token formats, protocols and procedures used to realize the GSS-API services on top of a particular security mechanism.

The mechanism provides authentication, key establishment, data integrity and data confidentiality in an on-line distributed application environment using a public-key infrastructure. Because it conforms to the interface defined in RFC 1508, SPKM can be used as a drop-in replacement by any application that makes use of security services through GSS-API calls, for example an application that already uses the Kerberos GSS-API mechanism. The use of a public-key infrastructure allows digital signatures supporting non-repudiation to be employed for message exchanges, and gives other benefits such as scalability to large user populations.

The background explains the design aims. SPKM allows both unilateral and mutual authentication without secure timestamps, so environments without access to secure time can still have secure authentication. It uses Algorithm Identifiers to specify the algorithms used by the communicating peers, which gives flexibility for different environments and for future enhancements. It allows the option of a true asymmetric digital signature in the sign and seal operations, rather than an integrity checksum computed with a symmetric algorithm, which some environments need for non-repudiation. The data formats and procedures are designed to be as similar as practical to those of the Kerberos mechanism, for ease of implementation where Kerberos already exists.

The document defines two mechanisms, SPKM-1 and SPKM-2, whose primary difference is that SPKM-2 requires secure timestamps for replay detection during context establishment and SPKM-1 does not. Typical use is expected to involve mutual authentication, and the use of unilateral authentication is not generally recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: An application asks for a secure channel without knowing how it will be made. SPKM is one of the answers to that question, built on certificates rather than on a password both sides already share.

sections.title: The Four Algorithm Slots
sections.content:
Four kinds of algorithm are used, and the peers negotiate which ones to use.

The integrity algorithm ensures that a message has not been altered after being constructed by the legitimate sender, and depending on the algorithm it may also provide authenticity and support non-repudiation. The examples are md5WithRSAEncryption, which is MANDATORY and computes an RSA signature on the MD5 hash of the data; DES-MAC, which is RECOMMENDED; md5-DES-CBC, which encrypts the confounded MD5 hash of the data with DES in CBC mode; and sum64-DES-CBC, which encrypts the confounded data together with the sum of all the input data blocks, computed modulo 2^64 - 1, so encryption is a requirement for the integrity to be secure. Because md5WithRSA is the only integrity algorithm stipulated as mandatory, it is also the algorithm used to sign all context establishment tokens that are signed rather than MACed.

The confidentiality algorithm is symmetric and generates the encrypted data for the seal and wrap calls; the example given is DES-CBC, which is RECOMMENDED. The key establishment algorithm establishes the symmetric key both sides use over the context: RSAEncryption is MANDATORY, in which the context key is generated by the initiator, encrypted with the target's RSA public key and sent to the target, so the target need not respond for the key to be established; id-rsa-key-transport is similar but also encrypts the source authenticating information; and dhKeyAgreement generates the context key jointly with the Diffie-Hellman algorithm, which means the target must respond, so it cannot be used with unilateral authentication in SPKM-2.

During context establishment the initiator offers a set of possible confidentiality algorithms and a set of possible integrity algorithms, and the target selects by returning, in the same relative order, the subset of each list it supports. Any of the agreed algorithms may be used for any message over the context, and the first algorithm in each agreed list becomes the default. The initiator also offers a set of possible key establishment algorithms along with the key or key half for the first one, its preferred algorithm; if the target cannot accept that one it must pick another from the set and send the choice along with the corresponding key or key half, or else send a delete token so the context is never established. The initiator also offers a set of possible one-way functions, and the target's choice becomes the subkey derivation function over the context.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side lists the algorithms it can do, the other side picks from that list, and both then know which ones are in use. The algorithms are named by their standard identifiers, so the two sides cannot talk past each other.

sections.title: Deriving the Subkeys
sections.content:
Having established a context key, both initiator and target must derive a set of subkeys for the confidentiality and keyed integrity algorithms agreed over the context. The agreed lists are numbered consecutively, the first algorithm being 0, and the context key is a binary string of arbitrary length M subject to the constraint that L is at most M and M is at most U, where L is the bit length of the longest key needed by any agreed confidentiality or keyed integrity algorithm and U is the largest bit size that fits within the key establishment parameters.

The RFC's example: if DES and two-key triple DES are the agreed confidentiality algorithms and DES-MAC the agreed keyed integrity algorithm, the context key must be at least 112 bits long. If 512-bit RSAEncryption is the key establishment algorithm in use, the originator can randomly generate a context key of any greater length up to 424 bits, the longest allowable RSA input, and the target determines the length chosen by removing the padding bytes during the RSA decryption. If dhKeyAgreement is in use, the context key is the result of the Diffie-Hellman computation with the exception of the high-order byte, which is discarded for security reasons, so its length is that of the Diffie-Hellman modulus minus 8 bits.

The derivation algorithm for a k-bit subkey is the rightmost k bits of the one-way function applied to the concatenation of the context key, a letter x, a number n, a stage s and the context key again. The letter x is the ASCII character C if the subkey is for a confidentiality algorithm and I if it is for a keyed integrity algorithm. The number n is the number of the algorithm in the agreed list, written as an ASCII digit. The stage s is always the ASCII character 0 unless k is greater than the output size of the one-way function, in which case the function is computed repeatedly with increasing ASCII values of the stage, each output being concatenated to the end of the previous outputs, until k bits have been generated.

Two one-way functions are given as examples. MD5 is MANDATORY. SHA is also named, and the RFC notes that existing hash functions may not satisfy all the required properties of one-way functions, which is why the choice is negotiated during context establishment: in that way future improvements in design can be accommodated.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides agree one secret key, then compute from it the separate keys each algorithm needs. The computation mixes in which algorithm the key is for, so the encryption key and the integrity key are never the same.

sections.title: Setting Up a Context
sections.content:
Three classes of token are defined for context establishment: Initiator tokens, emitted by gss_init_sec_context() and consumed by gss_accept_sec_context(); Target tokens, emitted by gss_accept_sec_context() and consumed by gss_init_sec_context(); and Error tokens, potentially emitted by either call and potentially consumed by either call.

The context establishment tokens are defined according to RFC 5280 Section 10. SPKM-1, which uses random numbers, uses the Two-way Authentication procedure when performing unilateral authentication of the target to the initiator, and the Three-way Authentication procedure when mutual authentication is requested. SPKM-2, which uses timestamps, uses the One-way Authentication procedure for unilateral authentication of the initiator to the target, and the Two-way Authentication procedure when mutual authentication is requested.

The implication is that for SPKM-2 unilateral authentication no negotiation of the key establishment algorithm can be done: the target either accepts the algorithm and context key given by the initiator or disallows the context. For SPKM-2 mutual or SPKM-1 unilateral authentication some negotiation is possible, but the target can only choose among the one-pass algorithms offered by the initiator. For SPKM-1 mutual authentication the target can choose any one-pass or two-pass algorithm offered, and can be requested to generate and transmit the context key.

A context establishment sequence performs unilateral authentication if the mutual-request bit is not set in the application's call to gss_init_sec_context(). SPKM-2 accomplishes this using only the SPKM-REQ token, authenticating the initiator to the target, while SPKM-1 uses both SPKM-REQ and SPKM-REP-TI, authenticating the target to the initiator. An application requiring authentication of both peers must request mutual authentication, which sets the mutual-state option in the SPKM-REQ token; the target then replies with an SPKM-REP-TI token, which completes the timestamp-based exchange for SPKM-2, while for SPKM-1 the initiator replies with an SPKM-REP-IT token, completing the random-number-based exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up the channel takes one, two or three messages depending on how much checking the application asked for and which of the two versions is in use.

sections.title: The Initiator's First Token
sections.content:
It may be necessary that both the initiator and the target have access to the other party's public-key certificates. In some environments the initiator may acquire all certificates and send the relevant ones in the first token; in others it may request that the target send certificate data in its response token, or each side may obtain the certificate data it needs. In any case the SPKM implementation must be able to obtain certificates which correspond to a supplied Name, and the mechanism for doing so is a local implementation matter.

The SPKM-REQ token carries a request token and optional certification data and authorization data. The certification data holds an optional certification path and an optional certificate revocation list, at least one of which must be present. The certification path can hold a user key identifier, a user certificate containing the user's public key, a verifier key identifier, a certificate containing the user's public verification key, and the CA certificates; having separate verification fields allows different key pairs, possibly for different algorithms, to be used for encryption and decryption and for signing and verification.

The request token itself holds the request contents, an Algorithm Identifier for the algorithm used, and the integrity value, which holds either the result of the signing procedure or the result of the MACing procedure depending on the algorithm named. The request contents carry a token identifier, which shall contain 0100 in hexadecimal, a context identifier that is a fresh random number, a protocol version number as a bit string with one bit per supported version, an optional timestamp that is mandatory for SPKM-2, a random number from the source, the target name, an optional source name that must be supplied unless the originator is anonymous, the context data, an optional validity interval, the set of key establishment algorithms, an optional key establishment parameter for the first of them, and an optional key-source binding.

The options carried in the context data are a bit string with delegation-state, mutual-state, replay-detect-state, sequence-state, conf-avail, integ-avail and target-certif-data-required. The key-source binding holds the result of applying MD5 to the concatenation of the DER-encoded source name and the context key, and it must be present for SPKM-2 unilateral authentication when the key establishment algorithm in use does not provide such a binding itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The first message says who you are, which algorithms you would like to use, the fresh random number that makes this exchange different from the last one, and a signed copy of all of it that the other side can check.

sections.title: Protecting Each Message
sections.content:
Three classes of token are defined here: MIC tokens, emitted by gss_getMIC() and consumed by gss_verifyMIC(); Wrap tokens, emitted by gss_wrap() and consumed by gss_unwrap(); and context deletion tokens, consumed by gss_process_context_token().

A MIC token holds a header and an integrity checksum, separate from the user data being protected. The application may send the token and the data separately and it is the receiving application's responsibility to associate them. The checksum is calculated over the data field, logically prepended by the bytes of the plaintext token header, so the result binds the data to the whole header and minimizes the possibility of malicious splicing. With md5WithRSA, an MD5 hash is computed over the plaintext data prepended by the header, and an RSA signature is computed on the 16-byte MD5 result. With a keyed algorithm such as DES-MAC, the key used is the appropriate subkey derived from the context key.

Sequence numbers are used for security rather than for reliability, to avoid malicious loss, replay or re-ordering of tokens, so applications are advised to request sequencing and replay detection over all contexts. The sequence number field is formed from the sender's four-byte sequence number and a Boolean direction indicator, false for the context initiator and true for the context acceptor, and is incremented by one after each token is constructed. The receiver compares the sequence number with the expected one: if it is higher the expected number is adjusted and GSS_S_GAP_TOKEN is returned, and if it is lower the expected number is not adjusted and a duplicate, out-of-sequence or old token status is returned. A wrong direction indicator returns the out-of-sequence status. Because the sequence number is part of the input to the integrity checksum, it need not be encrypted, and attempts to splice a checksum and sequence number from different messages are detected.

A Wrap token encapsulates the user data, optionally encrypted, along with the integrity check quantities. The token consists of an integrity header followed by a body holding either the plaintext data, if no confidentiality algorithm is in use, or encrypted data. As in Kerberos, an 8-byte random confounder is prepended to the data to compensate for the fact that an IV of zero is used for encryption. The checksum is calculated over the plaintext data field, logically prepended by the bytes of the plaintext token header, in the same way as for the MIC token.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a code that proves it was not altered, and optionally the message itself is scrambled. A counter in each message stops an attacker from replaying an old one or reflecting it back.

sections.title: Names and Object Identifiers
sections.content:
No mandatory name forms have yet been defined for SPKM; the section is left for further study. It does discuss name forms which may optionally be supported by implementations.

The User Name Form, with the recommended symbolic name GSS_SPKM_NT_USER_NAME, indicates a named user on a local system and its interpretation is specific to the operating system. The Machine UID Form, GSS_SPKM_NT_MACHINE_UID_NAME, indicates a numeric user identifier on a local system and holds a locally significant identifier in host byte order, which gss_import_name() resolves into a username that is then treated as the User Name Form. The String UID Form, GSS_SPKM_NT_STRING_UID_NAME, is similar but holds a string of digits representing that identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not require any particular way of naming a user. It offers three optional forms for implementations that want them, including one that resolves a numeric user ID into a name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that security issues are discussed throughout the memo. The parts that carry the security weight are the algorithm choices, where md5WithRSAEncryption is the only mandatory integrity algorithm and MD5 is the mandatory one-way function, and the rules that keep the exchange honest: fresh random numbers in every context, timestamps for SPKM-2, sequence numbers and a direction indicator in every per-message token, and the binding of the source name to the context key.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no separate section here, because the security points were already made where each mechanism is described.

messages.label: SPKM-REQ
messages.note: Signed, and carries the algorithm lists and the key establishment material.

messages.label: SPKM-REP-TI
messages.note: The target signs and returns its random number and the chosen algorithms.

messages.label: SPKM-REP-IT
messages.note: The initiator signs the target's random number, completing the exchange.

items.label: ERROR-TOKEN
items.desc: Reports an error during context establishment.

viz.caption: THE FOUR ALGORITHM SLOTS SPKM NEGOTIATES

items.title: Integrity
items.text: Detects changes to a message. md5WithRSAEncryption is mandatory.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: Encrypts the data. DES-CBC is recommended.

items.title: Key establishment
items.text: Agrees the shared context key. RSAEncryption is mandatory.

items.title: One-way function
items.text: Derives the subkeys from the context key. MD5 is mandatory.
